sources.excerpt: Defector by Foxpedal | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Foxpedal Defector LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS FUZZ OVERDRIVE BOOSTER Description FOR YOUR EYES ONLY: This former fuzz intelligence officer has snuck across our borders and is ready to trade state secrets for its freedom. Bringing with it all the fuzz it could pack in this little case, it packs a punch like no other. Classic Russian muff tones can certainly be had, but that's not what has the Kremlin sweating this breach. The independent "Pre" linear clean boost pushes the fuzz into full saturation at the touch of a button (notably, it also works standalone, but we really shouldn't leak that little secret to the public at large). Mid tones can be shaped from the full classic mid scoop, through flat mids all the way down to a mid hump. Classic silicon clipping gives you the breakup you know and love, switch to LED clipping for a more open attack, or (if you dare) go full Red Dawn by lifting the clipping diodes all together. Unbutton the hood and adjust the signal saturation via a trimpot on the PCB. And last but not least, enter the secret code to unlock the fuzz feedback mode -- a highly interactive and dare we say, dangerous, fuzz revolution. sources.excerpt: Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit By Liam Carter July 10, 2026 The Foxpedal Defector Fuzz is not another vintage-inspired clone—it’s a precision-engineered, modern analog fuzz pedal designed for dynamic responsiveness, harmonic fidelity, and studio-grade consistency. Measuring 118 mm × 68 mm × 52 mm (4.65″ × 2.68″ × 2.05″) with true-bypass switching and a discrete silicon transistor circuit (2N5088 and 2N5089 matched pair), it delivers 32 dB of gain with Design Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Foxpedal, based in Portland, Oregon, positions the Defector as a ‘fidelity-first’ fuzz. Its core departure from classic designs lies in intentional rejection of passive tone-sucking networks and unregulated bias drift. While most silicon fuzzes (e.g., Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi v1) use cascaded gain stages with RC filtering that attenuates low-end and compresses dynamics, the Defector employs a dual-stage active EQ buffer pre- and post-fuzz core. This architecture isolates the fuzz circuit from pickup impedance variations—a critical factor often overlooked in practice scenarios where players switch between Stratocasters (7.2 kΩ DC resistance) and Les Pauls (14.8 kΩ). Transistor Matching and Thermal Stability Each Defector unit ships with hand-matched 2N5088 (Q1, input stage) and 2N5089 (Q2, output stage) transistors, selected for h FE within ±3% tolerance (measured at V CE = 1V, I C = 1mA). This tight matching reduces inter-stage imbalance and ensures consistent clipping symmetry. Crucially, Foxpedal mounts both transistors on thermally coupled copper pads, achieving No Passive Tone Stack, No Compromise Many pedals insert passive tone controls (e.g., the treble bleed network in the Dunlop Fuzz Face) that load the circuit and degrade high-frequency transient response. The Defector omits such networks entirely. Instead, its single-knob ‘Tone’ control adjusts a fully active Baxandall-style EQ centered at 1.8 kHz, with ±12 dB boost/cut range and Q = 1.4. This preserves signal integrity while offering surgical shaping—essential when practicing legato phrasing or harmonic minor sequences where upper-mid clarity determines intelligibility. Key Controls and Operational Behavior The Defector features three knobs: Volume (output level, calibrated to unity at 12 o’clock), Fuzz (gain staging, logarithmic taper), and Tone (active EQ). All pots are Alpha 9mm sealed units rated for 200,000 cycles. Unlike pedals with ambiguous gain labeling (e.g., “Sustain” on the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff), the Fuzz control delivers linear, repeatable gain increase: from 18 dB at 9 o’clock to 32 dB at 3 o’clock, verified via oscilloscope measurement using a 1 kHz sine wave at −20 dBu input. Volume Control Precision The Volume knob operates with 0.5 dB resolution per 15° rotation near unity—meaning subtle adjustments (e.g., dropping volume by 1.5 dB for cleaner chord comping) are physically precise and audibly distinct. This granularity matters during metronome-based practice: reducing output by exactly 2 dB while maintaining identical pick attack allows focused study of dynamic shading without altering tonal character. Fuzz Knob Linearity and Sweet Spots At 10–2 o’clock, the Fuzz control yields a ‘transparent overdrive’ zone ideal for blues phrasing—retaining string texture and harmonic nuance. Between 2–4 o’clock, it transitions into singing sustain with even-order harmonic emphasis (measured 2nd harmonic at −14.2 dB relative to fundamental). From 4–6 o’clock, odd-order harmonics dominate (3rd at −12.8 dB), delivering articulate distortion suited for jazz-rock fusion lines.
